paragraphs.heading: The Moon in the way
paragraphs.text: A solar eclipse happens when the Moon moves between Earth and the Sun and blocks the Sun, fully or in part, from a small patch of Earth. In a total eclipse the Moon covers the whole disk of the Sun. Partial and annular eclipses hide just a portion of the Sun. A lunar eclipse can be seen from anywhere on Earth's night side, but a solar eclipse is visible only from a fairly small area.

paragraphs.heading: Three kinds of shadow
paragraphs.text: The Moon casts a shadow with distinct parts. The umbra is the dark core, where the Moon blocks the Sun completely; where it touches Earth's surface, a total eclipse can be seen. The penumbra is the wider, lighter shadow around it, where people see a partial eclipse. The antumbra is the shadow lying beyond the umbra, and anyone standing in it sees an annular eclipse.

paragraphs.heading: Why not every month
paragraphs.text: If the Moon circled Earth on a perfect circle in the same plane as Earth's orbit, every new moon would bring a total solar eclipse. In fact the Moon's orbit is tilted by just over 5 degrees to the ecliptic, the plane of Earth's orbit around the Sun. So at new moon the Moon usually slips past to the north or south of the Sun, and its shadow misses Earth. An eclipse can happen only when a new moon falls near a node, one of the two points where the Moon's path crosses the ecliptic.

paragraphs.heading: Eclipse seasons
paragraphs.text: The two nodes sit 180 degrees apart, so new moons line up near them in two stretches of the year, about 173.3 days apart, called eclipse seasons. Each season brings at least one solar eclipse. Sometimes a new moon falls close enough to a node in two months running, giving two partial eclipses in a row. As a result, every year has at least two solar eclipses and as many as five, but no more than two of them can be total.

paragraphs.heading: Total or annular
paragraphs.text: The Moon's orbit is an oval, and its distance from Earth swings by up to about 5.9% from the average. That changes how big it looks in our sky, and this is what decides between a total and an annular eclipse. On average the Moon looks 2.1% smaller than the Sun, so about 60% of central eclipses are annular. A total eclipse happens only when the Moon is nearer than average, close to its perigee.

paragraphs.heading: Rare in any one place
paragraphs.text: Somewhere on Earth, a total solar eclipse comes along every 18 months on average. Yet any given spot sees one only once every 360 to 410 years. Keen fans known as eclipse chasers, or umbraphiles, travel to remote places to see them. Looking straight at the Sun can permanently damage the eyes, so viewers need special eye protection or indirect methods, except during the total phase, which is safe to watch directly.

paragraphs.heading: Predicting eclipses
paragraphs.text: In some cultures, past and present, solar eclipses were blamed on supernatural forces or seen as bad omens. Astronomers in China were predicting eclipses as early as the 4th century BC. Today, eclipses hundreds of years ahead can be forecast with high accuracy.
